newsitem.title: GERMANY: Karstadt aims to treble 1997 net profit.
newsitem.headline: Karstadt aims to treble 1997 net profit.

text.p: German department store group Karstadt said on Wednesday it was on course to nearly treble net profits this year after earnings slid in 1996 and forced management to cut the dividend.

Chief executive Walter Deuss told the company's annual general meeting that five-month group earnings were in line with plans to achieve 1997 group net profits of around 150 million marks ($82 million), up from 58.6 million in 1996.

"Despite all the unknown factors in the forthcoming months and the uncertainty over the course of the important Christmas season, we are optimistic that we can reach our targets," Deuss said in a speech. He gave no interim earnings figures.
Karstadt has been hit by four years of falling consumer demand and the costly 1994 takeover and integration of the loss-making Hertie department store chain.

Deuss said, however, that although 11 Hertie stores faced closure or would be transferred to the Karstadt chain this year, the integration of the unit was "complete" and Hertie would near breakeven this year.

Karstadt will also pursue a strategy to remodel its stores along the lines of a theme-based pilot project in the city of Duisburg, where a store focusing on fashion has achieved sales growth of 10 percent on a product range reduced by 40 percent.
"The reaction of our customers has been extremely positive. The average amount that they spend is also much higher than the company average," Deuss said.

Deuss said another store had been upgraded in Rosenheim and refurbishment would be completed at Karstadt's Duesseldorf branch in October. He said the programme would be completed in two-and-a-half years but it was too early to estimate its cost.
Retail analysts have been following the Duisburg project with interest to see whether applying the revamp elsewhere would help boost profits dented by the Hertie takeover.

Deuss faced tough questioning from some shareholders over Karstadt's long-term profits decline and the failure to raise funds by selling the group's extensive property portfolio to invest in growing the business.

Another questioner said recent sharp gains in Karstadt's share price on takeover speculation was not exactly a vote of confidence in the management team led by Deuss -- who has been chief executive since 1979.
Both German holding company WCM and Dutch stores group Ahold last week denied being interested in taking over Karstadt, in which both Deutsche Bank AG and Commerzbank AG hold 10 percent each.
Despite the criticism, shareholders voted overwhelmingly to approve Karstadt's 1996 results and management's recommendation to cut the dividend payout to 10 marks from 13 marks.
Karstadt's stock closed on Wednesday on the Frankfurt stock exchange up 5.50 marks at 688 marks. Before the latest bout of bid reports the stock stood at 610 marks.

Deuss declined to comment on the takeover speculation, but did say that a management efficiency drive to streamline logistics would boost earnings by 150 million marks next year and by 250 million marks in 1998.

Karstadt also published sales figures for its units for the first half of the year, with parent firm Karstadt AG raising sales by 0.3 percent to 5.545 billion marks. On a same-store basis, however, sales were down by 3.3 percent.
At Hertie sales fell by 12.6 percent to 1.721 billion marks, while same-store sales were down by 5.3 percent.
Mail order unit Neckermann Versand AG posted half-year sales of 1.463 billion marks, down 1.9 percent on the same period a year earlier.
The Karstadt group's travel agency business increased sales in the first half to 419 million marks, up 3.9 percent. ($ = 1.829 German Marks)
